item.content:encoded:
(Commentary)
Here's the thing about all the agita related to the Los Angeles Dodgers, MLB's competitive balance and the 2026 postseason: No outcome this October will change the calculus for the team owners.
Even if the small-market Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians win the World Series, the league will continue its push for a salary cap, contending the sport lacks sufficient parity and is effectively broken.
Not that long ago, the league was making precisely the opposite argument. Its public-relations department, in news releases before the 2021 and 2022 seasons, described competitive balance as a hallmark of MLB.
Let's be clear: Revenue disparity between large- and small-market clubs is a legitimate concern. The league and players union need to adopt significant measures to make the playing field more level. But the league's argument for greater competitive balance, if not a red herring, is at least an argument of convenience. And not a particularly strong one, if you watched the regular season.
The Brewers finished with the best record in the National League. The Rays produced the best record in the American League. And the Guardians became the third small-market team to earn one of four first-round byes. Perhaps the Guardians were undeserving, considering their record was only the 11th best in the majors. But by finishing with the second-best mark among AL division winners, they clinched the bye under the postseason format the league and union created.
So is the sport really that far gone?
The league's own news release in 2022 noted that MLB produced 15 different World Series champions in the prior 21 seasons. The Texas Rangers in 2023 made it 16. And before the 2024 World Series, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred told The Athletic, "Our record on competitive balance is darn good."
Just two years later, to hear Manfred & Co. tell it, the sport is having an existential crisis. All because the league's highest-revenue team, the Dodgers, won back-to-back World Series. All because the team owners want to build their case for a cap.
The league cites a need for greater competitive balance as justification to drastically overhaul the game's economic system. And it is trumpeting a new set of facts -- specifically, the absence of a small-market champion since the 2015 Kansas City Royals -- to make its case.
There is no denying that in that time, large-market teams have accounted for 90% of World Series winners, 85% of World Series participants and 77.5% of league championship series participants. And sure, the same pattern might continue this year.
Never mind that the Dodgers performed below expectations in the regular season for the second consecutive year. According to FanGraphs, they still stand the best chance of winning the World Series -- 36.7%, with the Brewers next at 11.6%. As if on cue, and in some cases by design, the Dodgers' best players are getting healthy and rounding into form.
If Los Angeles becomes the first team since the 1998 to 2000 New York Yankees to win three consecutive World Series titles, the league will surely use that data point in its pitch that only a salary cap can save the sport.
And if the Brewers or Rays win their first Series, or if the Guardians win their first since 1948? The league will consider it an aberration, a single-season outcome that means little when compared with the larger sample size of the previous 10 seasons. An exception that proves the rule.
But let's broaden the discussion.
By emphasizing postseason results, the league is devaluing the most accurate measure of a club, the six-month grind of the regular season. Not to mention devaluing the 162 games of inventory all 30 clubs must sell.
Since 2015 -- the line of demarcation the league has set with the Royals' World Series triumph -- the Guardians rank fourth in regular-season wins, the Brewers fifth and the Rays seventh. They are models for other small-market teams, proof that those clubs do not have to operate without hope.
It's true none of those teams won a World Series in the past 10 years. But the Rays got there in the shortened 2020 season. The Guardians reached the American League Championship Series in 2024, the Brewers in 2025. Inferior depth, resulting in part from lower payrolls, might be part of the reason none went further. Adjustments to the collective bargaining agreement could help address that.
No reasonable person would start a league from scratch and adopt baseball's current economic system, in which the league says that the top four spenders -- the Dodgers, New York Mets, Yankees and Philadelphia Phillies -- outspent the bottom 22 in free agency over the course of the current labor agreement.
Reasonable people can disagree, however, whether a cap is the only possible solution when the players' historic opposition to the concept might lead to the cancellation of part or all of the 2027 season.
The league keeps referencing polls saying fans want a cap. Fans, though, evidently are not too upset with the current state of affairs: The league's attendance increased again this year, reaching its highest level since 2016.
Even in cap sports, not every team begins every season with the expectation of competing for a title. The most successful franchises are the shrewdest. Part of baseball's problem is that innovative small-market clubs no longer hold the competitive advantage they once did over less forward-thinking opponents.
Ex // Top Stories
Some of the large-market teams plucked top small-market executives. Very few clubs, if any, continue to lag behind in the intellectual arms race. Even the Colorado Rockies and Washington Nationals, two of the slowest clubs to adapt to baseball's information age, have gotten smarter.
If everyone is essentially working off the same data, payrolls become more of a separator. But even then, the edge money provides is not an absolute guarantee of success in October.
Before winning in the shortened 2020 season, the Dodgers had not won a World Series since 1988. The Mets have not won since 1986. The Phillies and Yankees are experiencing championship droughts that began in 2008 and 2009.
Many baseball executives consider the postseason a crapshoot, fearing the random outcomes that occur in small samples.
The Dodgers, without question, have inordinate financial advantages, including the right to withhold a healthy portion of their massive local TV deal from revenue sharing, a benefit that arose from a settlement the league reached in bankruptcy court with the team's former owner Frank McCourt.
Still, the Dodgers in 2022 and 2023 were eliminated in the division series by rivals from smaller markets, the San Diego Padres and Arizona Diamondbacks. In 2024, the Dodgers' first year with Shohei Ohtani, they nearly lost to the Padres again in division series play. And if not for a series of fortuitous events, they would have lost the 2025 World Series to the Toronto Blue Jays.
Another thing lost in the discussion about the Dodgers' dominance is that villains are good for business. This is the third consecutive season the Dodgers led the majors in road attendance. Their spending forces other NL clubs to try to keep pace. The small-market Padres, in particular, are better for it.
Yet the ability to spend is sometimes a double-edged sword. Long-term contracts sometimes backfire. Seemingly capable of papering over any mistake by simply printing more money, the Dodgers roll merrily along even when free-agent additions such as Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz and Tanner Scott slump. But several of the Dodgers' biggest and most expensive stars are facing age-related decline. A number of other top-10 payroll clubs, including the Padres, are locked into the same kinds of players.
None of that means that the league and union should proceed as if all is well, assuming the game's cyclical nature will balance things out. The concerns of the small-market clubs must be addressed, and the union acknowledged as much in May with its initial proposals, some of which addressed revenue disparity.
The union proposed enhanced revenue sharing that included protections "to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering"; financial rewards for successful revenue-sharing recipients and draft-pick incentives for them to sign free agents and retain their own players on the verge of hitting the open market.
The league scoffed at the union proposals, as one might expect with the collective bargaining agreement months away from expiration and the parties holding completely different worldviews. Finding a middle ground will be tricky. At least to this point, large-market clubs are willing to share more revenue -- and yield their inherent financial advantages -- but only under a cap system that fixes their costs.
Teams like the Brewers, Rays and Guardians clearly do not require more money to win regular-season games. But the way they operate, frequently trading stars as they get closer to free agency, is far from fan-friendly. Brewers fans buying a Jacob Misiorowski jersey and Rays fans buying a Junior Caminero jersey know not to get too attached to those players. As one small-market executive says: "Championships are won with talent, continuity and experience. We can get talent. The other two are tough to come by."
Tough, but not impossible. Countless examples exist of revenue-sharing recipients signing homegrown players for the long term. The Brewers did it with Jackson Chourio, Cooper Pratt and Luis Lara, the Guardians with José Ramírez and Tanner Bibee. The Pittsburgh Pirates might not keep Paul Skenes, but they locked up Konnor Griffin. The Royals secured extensions with Bobby Witt Jr. and Maikel Garcia, the Seattle Mariners with Cal Raleigh and Julio Rodríguez, the Arizona Diamondbacks with Corbin Carroll and Geraldo Perdomo.
Based on its proposals, the union thinks giving small-market teams an even better opportunity to retain players would benefit the sport. A salary cap is not necessary to make those adjustments and others to the collective bargaining agreement. Much as the league would like fans to believe otherwise, this is not an all-or-nothing situation.
In June, a reporter asked Manfred why he portrays a league he described in 2024 as having a "darn good" record on competitive balance to be out of whack just two years later.
"In the context, particularly of the postseason, where you're trying to generate interest and maximize viewership, I think it's important to emphasize competitiveness," Manfred said. "And there are aspects of competitiveness."
He added: "When we think about it from a labor perspective, we're focused on an entirely different part of the calendar. And that's the offseason, when you're trying to sell season tickets, and the perception among our fans that's really strong that we have a lack of competitiveness."
Maximizing viewership in the postseason? Viewership in the United States last year was the sport's highest since 2017. Selling season tickets? Sure, it's a problem in markets where team owners do not adequately invest in their franchises. It should be less of a problem in places like Milwaukee, Tampa Bay and Cleveland, if we're just talking about the product.
Make the current system fairer, and those clubs will stand even better chances of reaching a postseason that the league expanded to 12 teams from 10 in 2022. Give those clubs enough cracks at the postseason, and eventually one or more will break through.
It could happen this year, if the Brewers, Rays or Guardians win the World Series. The system needs improvement, no doubt. But if competitive balance is the object, it's a lot closer than it appears.

item.title: [MLB.com] Sale looks to 'harness the energy' in Braves postseason debut
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- When Walt Weiss sends Chris Sale to the mound for Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon, he’ll have the same confidence he possessed more than a quarter of a century ago, when he was playing behind John Smoltz, Tom Glavine and Greg Maddux in postseason games. “There’s a different feeling when a guy like that is taking the mound,” Weiss said. “We felt it those years with the Big Three, and I felt it at other times in my career. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- When Walt Weiss sends Chris Sale to the mound for Game 1 of the National League Wild Card Series on Tuesday afternoon, he’ll have the same confidence he possessed more than a quarter of a century ago, when he was playing behind John Smoltz, Tom Glavine and Greg Maddux in postseason games.
“There’s a different feeling when a guy like that is taking the mound,” Weiss said. “We felt it those years with the Big Three, and I felt it at other times in my career. I felt it in Oakland with Dave Stewart. I think it elevates the room the day that guy is pitching.”
Weiss made three straight trips to the playoffs as Atlanta’s shortstop from 1998-2000, and he’s experienced the postseason seven of the past eight years as the team’s bench coach. So, Braves playoff baseball is nothing new for him.
But, for Sale, this will be an experience he has long awaited.
The 37-year-old left-hander’s back prevented him from pitching in the postseason during his 2024 NL Cy Young Award season. But the splendid year he has produced during this third season with Atlanta will be enriched when he throws the first pitch of this Wild Card Series against the Phillies on Tuesday at 2 p.m. ET (NBC/Peacock).
“I love pitching here in Atlanta,” Sale said. “I love pitching in front of these fans, and being able to do it in the postseason makes it that much more special.”
Sale’s greatest postseason moment occurred when he concluded the 2018 World Series for the Red Sox by striking out each of the three batters he faced in the ninth inning of Game 5. His most recent playoff experience occurred in 2021, when, two months after returning from Tommy John surgery, he made three frustrating starts for Boston.
Five years later, Sale is in a far different position. After injuries limited him to a total of 151 innings from 2020-23, the Red Sox essentially gave up on him and sent him to Atlanta prior to the 2024 season. The lanky lefty flourished that year, and has continued to get better. The 2.16 ERA he produced this year ranked third in MLB, and it stands as the fifth-best mark produced by any Braves pitcher who has made at least 25 starts in any season going back to 1920.
So, there truly is reason to think this year’s postseason experience might be different. Sale has constructed a 7.24 ERA in seven previous playoff starts. His struggles weren’t restricted to the 2021 experience. He posted a 6.87 ERA in the four postseason starts he made in 2017 and ‘18. He allowed seven earned runs in one and lasted fewer than five innings in two others.
“I think you learn that it's just about harnessing the energy,” Sale said. “I learned this from David Tollett, my college coach [at Florida Gulf Coast University] -- you can't be better than you are. You can't play above what you possess, and sometimes you go out there and try to do too much, and actually do less.”
The opponents and pitching matchups Sale drew over the past two months prepared him for what he could encounter over the next few weeks. While posting a 2.36 ERA over his final seven starts, he pitched against four playoff teams (Yankees, Brewers, Dodgers and twice against the Phillies) and one (D-backs) that nearly made the postseason.
Within this same stretch, Sale matched up against top-flight starters Gerrit Cole, Jacob Misiorowski, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Cristopher Sánchez and Aaron Nola.
“He’s been nothing short of amazing for us,” Braves first baseman Matt Olson said. “I wouldn’t want anybody else taking the mound for us tomorrow.”
Sale certainly has reason to enter this assignment with confidence. He posted a 2.08 ERA in four starts against the Phillies this season, and the Braves won each of those contests.
If he can garner similar results on Tuesday, there’s a good chance this won’t be the only postseason start he will make this year.
“He presents a whole set of problems, but we've seen him a [few times],” Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. “We haven't been great with him, but we'll see. Tomorrow is a new day.”

item.title: [yardbarker.com] Predicting all MLB postseason rounds: Who wins the World Series?
item.dc:creator: Kevin Henry
item.description: As the 2026 MLB postseason prepares to begin, it's a good time for some bold predictions about who will win and why, from the wild-card rounds to the World Series. item.content:encoded:
As the 2026 MLB postseason prepares to begin, it's a good time for some bold predictions about who will win and why, from the wild-card rounds to the World Series.
Chicago White Sox at Houston Astros
Houston was just 11-13 in September and it felt like neither the Astros nor the Texas Rangers wanted to win the AL West. Houston finally did on the last day, but the Astros aren't inspiring confidence that they can go deep into the postseason.
The White Sox could have been the AL Central champs, but couldn't hang on as Cleveland made a hard charge and overtook them. For a team that has been told all season about they are still living in the shadow of a 121-loss season two years ago, this team has a chip on its shoulder. That should push the White Sox into the next round.
Boston Red Sox at New York Yankees
After a chaotic weather weekend in the Northeast that forced the Red Sox to play Game 162 in Tampa and canceled the final game of the season for the Yankees, that extra day of rest (and far less travel) may help New York when the wild-card series opens in the Bronx.
New York's pitching lineup of Cam Schlittler, Max Fried and Gerrit Cole will be enough to overcome any of the Yankees' offensive issues in a series that will last just two games.
Philadelphia Phillies at Atlanta Braves
Like Houston, Philadelphia did little to inspire confidence in its postseason future at the end of the regular season. It's also been a season where the Braves have Philadelphia's number, winning nine of the 13 games the two rivals have played. Atlanta sweeps Philadelphia.
Chicago Cubs at San Diego Padres
The Padres are red-hot entering the wild card, going 18-6 in September to secure a home series. Having the home fans on their side, San Diego will continue its solid play by sweeping the Cubs into the offseason.
New York Yankees vs. Tampa Bay Rays
While the Yankees may have had enough to get into the ALDS, there's little doubt that the Rays are the better team.
All season, it was a question of if New York could catch Tampa Bay for the AL East title. The Rays kept showing they weren't going to crack under any pressure, and that continues with a 3-1 series win to move on to the ALCS.
Chicago White Sox vs. Cleveland Guardians
Chicago's story has been incredible, but there's a reason why the Guardians won the division ... and keep a reputation as the team that doesn't die easily. They're built for pressure and the postseason and will dispatch the White Sox in four games.
Atlanta Braves vs. Los Angeles Dodgers
This will be must-see TV as two of the NL's behemoths battle it out. The home advantage will make a difference for the Dodgers, who will win in Game 5 to seal another trip to the NLCS.
San Diego Padres vs. Milwaukee Brewers
Milwaukee is for real. There have been plenty of instances in the past where the Brewers have stumbled in the postseason, but this won't be a repeat of those mistakes. Jacob Misiorowski will set the tone in the first game and the Brewers will win in four.
Tampa Bay Rays vs. Cleveland Guardians
The Rays went 5-1 against Cleveland this season. With homefield advantage, there's no reason to think that trend won't continue. Look for the Rays to oust the Guardians in six games.
Los Angeles Dodgers vs. Milwaukee Brewers
This season, the Brewers are 4-3 against the Dodgers. With Milwaukee holding home-field advantage, this is the year that Los Angeles is finally stopped short of winning it all.
There is a lot to like for Milwaukee in their relief pitching options, and it may come down to that. While the Dodgers may have the better rotation, Milwaukee has the better pitching staff overall. Pitching wins in October, and the Brewers win a classic in seven games in front of their home fans.
Tampa Bay Rays vs. Milwaukee Brewers
A World Series without a "major market" in it? Oh this will set up plenty of conversations for what will be a contentious offseason.
Neither of these teams have won a World Series, making for another fascinating storyline in what will be an epic Fall Classic. Milwaukee has the home-field advantage thanks to their 103 regular-season wins, and that makes a big difference in this battle of the top seeds.
Brewers in six.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Brewers' Misiorowski Makes 76-Year-Old MLB History
item.dc:creator: Jordon Lawrenz
item.description: Since 1950, there have only been four pitchers to lead the league in ERA, strikeouts, and opponents' batting average. item.content:encoded:
Since 1950, there have only been four pitchers to lead the league in ERA, strikeouts, and opponents' batting average.
Here in 2026, Milwaukee Brewers' ace Jacob Misiorowski officially joined that list.
Misiorowski now finds himself in the same conversation as Sandy Koufax (1965), J.R. Richard (1979), and Mike Scott (1986), according to the Elias Sports Bureau.
The Brewers' regular season ended the exact same way it started, and that was with Misiorowski picking up a win.
His 16th win of the year was a nearly flawless 5.1-inning performance, one that proved this 24-year-old has what it takes to help the Brewers make a deep run in the postseason.
Misiorowski caps off historic 2026 season
Going back 76 years, Miz joins an exclusive club that features a few all-time greats. To think this accomplishment hasn't been done since 1986 is even more incredible, especially knowing how many stellar pitchers have won the Cy Young and taken the world by storm since then.
Misiorowski made 30 starts this season as he posted league-best numbers in strikeouts (252), ERA (1.80), and opponents' batting average (.157).
Those obviously aren't the only statistics that he led the league in, but those are the three that helped him make history dating back to 1950.
Misiorowski's speed is unheard of
For a starting pitcher to be able to throw 100+ miles per hour consistently is something that isn't seen too often in the modern era.
Sure, having a closer come in and throw that is one thing, but to see Misiorowski do it as consistently as he did was another.
Officially, his 1,115 pitches at 100+ mph this season were the most since tracking started in 2008. Previously, the record was set by Jordan Hicks in 2018, but he only threw 673 that year.
To say "only" in that sentence proves just how out-of-this-world Misiorowski's stuff truly is.
His regular season came to an end with 174.2 innings thrown, so that comes out to roughly 6.4 pitches of 100+ mph thrown per inning.
Brewers are hungry for a World Series
Keep in mind, Misiorowski appeared out of the bullpen in three postseason games a year ago. He was 2-1 and sported a 1.50 ERA and 0.83 WHIP in his 12 innings pitched.
Misiorowski had a 5.3 K/BB ratio in a limited sample size last year, so it's incredible to think that number was 5.7 here in the regular season.
If there's anyone who can help guide the Brewers to a World Series, it's Misiorowski, and now he gets some much-needed rest as this team went 103-59 and is able to skip the Wild Card round for the second straight season.

item.title: [coloradostar.com] MLB roundup: Astros blank A's, capture AL West title

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

28 Sep 2026, 10:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Ed Szczepanski)
Rookie Lucas Spence ripped a two-run triple to highlight a four-run third inning, helping the Houston Astros celebrate the American League West title with a 9-0 victory over the Athletics on Sunday in West Sacramento, Calif.
Christian Walker homered to lead off the sixth inning and joined Yainer Diaz, Cam Smith and Jeremy Pena in collecting two hits and an RBI for the Astros (81-81), who won the division for the eighth time in the last 10 seasons.
Third-seeded Houston will host the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Game 1 of the best-of-three wild-card series. The Astros went 5-2 against the White Sox this season.
Houston actually captured the AL West title prior to the conclusion of its victory, as the Texas Rangers dropped a 6-4 decision to the Minnesota Twins on Sunday.
Yordan Alvarez went 1-for-4 with an RBI single to boost his batting average to .316, giving him his first batting title.
Lawrence Butler had two of the five hits for the Athletics (64-98), who lost for the ninth time in 12 games.
Phillies 7, Tampa Bay 3
Zack Wheeler pitched six strong innings and Kyle Schwarber drove in two runs as the Phillies clinched their fifth straight postseason berth by beating the Rays.
Bryce Harper and Edmundo Sosa homered for Philadelphia, which had lost its previous four games by the combined score of 23-3. The Phillies finally showed signs of life in Game 162, and now they'll head to Atlanta to face the Braves in the National League wild-card round that begins on Tuesday,
Johnny DeLuca homered twice for Tampa Bay. The Rays earned a bye into the American League Division Series and face the winner of the wild-card series between the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox.
Cubs 6, Red Sox 2
Alex Bregman went 4-for-4 with two home runs and four RBIs against his former team to help Chicago wrap up the regular season by defeating Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The game was scheduled to be played in Boston, but was moved to Tropicana Field because of the nor'easter that hit much of New England throughout the weekend.
Both of Bregman's home runs came against Boston starter Tanner Houck, who made his first appearance on the mound since May 2025. Houck (0-1), who had Tommy John surgery last year, allowed three runs on four hits in three innings. The Red Sox were held to five hits and were 0-for-7 with runners in scoring position.
Twins 6, Rangers 4
Josh Bell hit a two-run home run and drove in three to lead host Minnesota to a season-ending win over Texas.
The loss eliminated the Rangers from the American League West title race and the playoffs. Rangers starter Mackenzie Gore allowed one hit and one run in 2 1/3 innings.
Twins starter Dean Kremer (5-5) gave up three hits and one run in seven innings. Kremer yielded a home run to Danny Jansen, but did not allow another Texas runner past first base.
Dodgers 5, Giants 1 (10 innings)
Andy Pages capped a four-run 10th inning with a three-run home run, and visiting Los Angeles beat San Francisco to earn its 100th win of the season.
The Dodgers took the lead in the 10th when Alex Call's two-out double off the left field fence drove in automatic runner Miguel Rojas. The Giants then elected to walk Max Muncy, before Pages foiled that strategy by driving a pitch by Duncan Davitt (0-1) into the left field bleachers for his 23rd home run of the season.
Alex Vesia (3-1), whose perfect ninth sent the game into the 10th, was credited with the win, which allows the Dodgers to take a three-game winning streak into their National League Division Series opener next Saturday against the winner of the wild-card series between the host Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies.
Marlins 5, Braves 3
Heriberto Hernandez and Griffin Conine slugged solo home runs, giving host Miami a win over Atlanta to end its season on a high note.
Marlins ace Sandy Alcantara tossed a scoreless ninth inning for his third career save. It was a fitting end of the year for Alcantara, who threw both the first and last pitch of the season for Miami. sStarter Janson Junk left with a no-decision. He allowed three hits and one run in 4 2/3 innings. Michael Petersen (4-4) earned the win with 1 1/3 hitless innings of relief.
Braves starter JR Ritchie (1-5) took the loss. He allowed seven hits and four runs in 5 2/3 innings. Mauricio Dubon hit his 12th homer to open the scoring and added an RBI single for Atlanta, which begins its home wild-card series against divisional rival Philadelphia on Tuesday.
Nationals 6, Mets 4
Andres Chaparro had three hits, including two solo home runs, and host Washington beat New York to end its season with a series win.
Will Dion (3-2) pitched two scoreless innings for the victory and Erik Tolman worked the ninth for his fifth save for Washington, which improved by 11 wins over 2025.
Francisco Lindor hit his 300th career homer and Ronny Mauricio smacked his third home run in two games for the Mets, who finished last in the National League East. Carson Benge ended his rookie season with three hits and an RBI.
Blue Jays 5, Reds 1
In potentially his final career start, Max Scherzer struck out seven over seven-plus innings and host Toronto topped Cincinnati.
The 42-year-old Scherzer (4-9) allowed one run and six hits to earn his 225th career win and boost his strikeout total to 3,557. The Blue Jays' 37-year-old designated hitter George Springer, who might have also played his last game, like Scherzer received a standing ovation when he was replaced.
Brandon Valenzuela hit a two-run home run for Toronto and Charles McAdoo added a solo shot in the rubber match of the three-game series. Brandon Williamson (5-5) allowed four runs and four hits in three innings for the Reds.
White Sox 4, Rockies 2
Randal Grichuk and Brenton Doyle smacked two-run home runs and Anthony Kay pitched five strong innings to boost host Chicago past Colorado.
The White Sox are set to visit the American League West champion Houston Astros on Tuesday in the opener of an AL wild-card series. Chicago clinched its first playoff berth on Thursday since 2021 but was eliminated from contention for an AL Central title with Saturday's loss to Colorado and a Cleveland victory at Kansas City.
Cole Carrigg homered for Colorado, which finished with more than 100 losses for the fourth successive season.
Royals 3, Guardians 2
Vinnie Pasquantino's second solo homer of the day broke an eighth-inning tie and sent host Kansas City to a win over Cleveland.
Jac Caglianone and Kyle Isbel each had two hits for the Royals, who ended a disappointing 2026 campaign by avoiding a sweep and winning for just the seventh time in the final 25 games.
Daniel Schneemann and Jo Adell each homered and had two hits apiece for the Guardians, who rested key regulars Steven Kwan, Jose Ramirez and Brayan Rocchio one day after securing their third consecutive American League Central title. Cleveland plays either the Chicago White Sox or Houston Astros in the American League Division Series.
Pirates 4, Tigers 2
Jared Jones pitched four innings of one-hit ball and Konnor Griffin led off the game with a solo home run and drove in two runs to lead Pittsburgh past host Detroit.
Griffin's homer was the sixth of his rookie season and helped the Pirates secure their first winning record since 2018 and only their second since last making the postseason in 2015. Jones was not eligible for the win after exiting the game before the fifth. Jones finished 5-6 with a 3.72 ERA in 21 starts after returning from elbow surgery in late May.
Rookie River Ryan (0-1) made his second start for the Tigers and sixth of his career. The right-hander allowed two runs on three hits over 1 1/3 innings. Detroit finished with a losing record after advancing to the American League Division Series each of the past two seasons.
Padres 9, Diamondbacks 4
Gavin Sheets homered and Freddy Fermin knocked in three runs as host San Diego tuned up for their National League wild-card series by stopping visiting Arizona.
San Diego, which opens its best-of-three series Tuesday night against the visiting Chicago Cubs, snapped a 4-4 tie with three runs in the bottom of the seventh. Fermin capped it with a two-run single.
Michael Soroka pitched 4 2/3 innings for Arizona, which was eliminated from postseason contention when Philadelphia beat Tampa Bay around the same time San Diego's Jake Cronenworth drew a bases-loaded walk to push home the go-ahead run in the seventh.
Brewers 6, Cardinals 4
Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his case for the National League Cy Young Award, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as host Milwaukee beat St. Louis to close with five consecutive wins and its franchise record for victories in a season (103).
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings and lowered his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. The right-hander struck out five, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Cardinals starter Andre Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings. He allowed six singles in the first inning for a 3-0 Brewers lead as well as Gary Sanchez's home run in the third.
Mariners 7, Angels 4
Logan Gilbert pitched four-plus hitless innings and struck out eight as host Seattle dealt Los Angeles its 100th loss of the season. It was also the last game for Dan Wilson as the Mariners' manager. The team announced after the game that Wilson will not return in that role in 2027 after a disappointing season and third-place finish in the American League West.
Jose Siri homered for the Angels, losers of 100 games for the first time. They had been the lone active MLB team to never suffer that many defeats.
Gilbert didn't allow a baserunner until walking Moises Ballesteros leading off the fifth. He struck out the side in the first inning to reach 200 strikeouts for the season, becoming the fourth pitcher in franchise history to do so in multiple seasons.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [MLB.com] Misiorowski brilla para sellar una de las campañas más dominantes en la historia
item.dc:creator: Adam McCalvy
item.description: MILWAUKEE -- Cada día de apertura era un evento cuando Jacob Misiorowski se subía al montículo durante la temporada regular de 103 victorias de los Cerveceros, una cifra récord para la franquicia. Hasta el último encuentro. item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- Cada día de apertura era un evento cuando Jacob Misiorowski se subía al montículo durante la temporada regular de 103 victorias de los Cerveceros, una cifra récord para la franquicia. Hasta el último encuentro.
El as de 24 años de Milwaukee recibió una ovación mientras trotaba hacia el dugout para calentar, y otra cuando salió del montículo tras su último calentamiento de cara a la postemporada en la victoria de los Cerveceros por 6-4 el domingo en el American Family Field, tras ponchar al estelar guardabosque de los Cardenales, Jordan Walker, para cerrar con broche de oro una de las campañas más dominantes en la historia.
Con 5.1 entradas en blanco adicionales de dos hits y dos boletos, con cinco ponches y una recta que alcanzó hasta las 102.7 mph, el as de 6 pies 7 pulgadas de los Cerveceros terminó como el líder de las Grandes Ligas en efectividad (1.80), ponches (252), WHIP (0.80) y promedio de sus oponentes (.157) en 174.2 electrizantes entradas.
Se unió a Corbin Burnes (2021) como los únicos lanzadores en la historia de la franquicia de Milwaukee en ganar el título de efectividad de MLB, y se unió a Justin Verlander (2019) y al dominicano Pedro Martínez (2000) como los únicos serpentineros en la historia con más de 250 ponches y WHIP de al menos 0.80. Y según Elias Sports Bureau, Misiorowski se unió a Sandy Koufax (1965), J.R. Richard (1976) y Mike Scott (1986) como los únicos pitchers desde 1950 en encabezar las Mayores en efectividad, ponches y promedio de sus oponentes.
Podrías seguir señalando estadísticas. Los Cerveceros terminaron con el mejor récord en todo el béisbol con 103-59, y no hubo duda alguna sobre quién encabezó el cuerpo de pitcheo.
Aquí hay algunas otras medidas récord de lanzadores que registraron al menos 170 entradas en una temporada:
Tasa de ponches
- 39.9% Gerrit Cole (2019)
- 37.9% Misiorowski (2026)
- 37.5% Pedro Martínez (1999)
- 37.4% Randy Johnson (2001)
- 36.8% Spencer Strider (2023)
WHIP
- 0.74 Pedro Martínez (2000)
- 0.78 Walter Johnson (1913)
- 0.80 Misiorowski (2026)
- 0.80 Justin Verlander (2019)
- 0.81 Addie Joss (1908)
Promedio de sus oponentes
- .157 Misiorowski (2026)
- .167 Pedro Martínez (2000)
- .168 Luis Tiant (1968)
- .171 Nolan Ryan (1972)
- .172 Nolan Ryan (1991)
- .172 Justin Verlander (2019)
Para la efectividad, usaremos 1969 como punto de partida, debido a que fue el año en que MLB bajó el montículo a su altura actual en respuesta al Año del Lanzador en 1968. Aquí es donde encaja Misiorowski entre las mejores efectividades desde entonces entre serpentineros que registraron al menos 170 episodios:
- 1.53 Dwight Gooden (1985)
- 1.56 Greg Maddux (1994)
- 1.63 Greg Maddux (1995)
- 1.66 Zack Greinke (2015)
- 1.70 Jacob deGrom (2018)
- 1.74 Pedro Martínez (2000)
- 1.74 Ron Guidry (1978)
- 1.75 Justin Verlander (2022)
- 1.76 Tom Seaver (1971)
- 1.77 Jake Arrieta (2015)
- 1.80 Misiorowski (2026)
- 1.82 Vida Blue (1971)
- 1.83 Clayton Kershaw (2014)
- 1.87 Roger Clemens (2005)

item.title: [Field Level Media] Jacob Misiorowski makes Cy Young case as Brewers down Cardinals
item.description: Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his Cy Young case, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as the Milwaukee Brewers built momentum for the postseason with a 6-4 victory over the visiting St. Louis Cardinals on Sunday. Milwaukee (103-59), which has clinched a first-round Wild Card bye and home-field advantage throughout the playoffs, closed with five consecutive wins to extend its franchise record for victories in a season. Milwaukee, the first team to win four consecutive NL Cent
item.content:encoded:
Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his Cy Young case, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as the Milwaukee Brewers built momentum for the postseason with a 6-4 victory over the visiting St. Louis Cardinals on Sunday.
Milwaukee (103-59), which has clinched a first-round Wild Card bye and home-field advantage throughout the playoffs, closed with five consecutive wins to extend its franchise record for victories in a season.
Milwaukee, the first team to win four consecutive NL Central titles, finished 35-17 against division rivals and went 18-6 in September.
St. Louis (77-85) scored four runs in the eighth off Chad Patrick to pull within 6-4, capped by Leo Bernal’s three-run homer. Shane Drohan got the final five outs for his second save.
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings, departing after striking out Jordan Walker in the sixth to end a 68-pitch outing, lowering his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. Misiorowski struck out five and walked two, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Misiorowski is the second Brewers pitcher to lead the league in ERA, joining Corbin Burnes (2021).
Milwaukee bunched six singles off Andre Pallante in the first inning for a 3-0 lead. Garrett Mitchell, Jake Bauers and Jackson Chourio opened with consecutive singles for the first run. Brice Turang reached on a run-scoring infield single, giving him 100 RBIs for the season. Christian Yelich singled in another run.
Gary Sanchez put the Brewers up 5-0 with one out in the third with his 12th home run following a leadoff single by Chourio.
Chourio’s RBI single in the fourth made it 6-0.
St. Louis rallied in the eighth when Cesar Prieto triple to open and Pedro Pages walked. Prieto scored on Jordan Walker’s fielder’s choice grounder. Ivan Herrera walked and Bernal followed with his fifth homer.
Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings, striking out four and walking one.
St. Louis, which has not made the postseason since 2022 and has not won a playoff series since the NLDS in 2019, was 50-45 at the All-Star break, but went 27-40 the rest of the way.
–Field Level Media

item.title: [WMTV 15 NEWS] Misiorowski continues Cy Young Award push and Turang gets 100th RBI as Brewers beat Cardinals 6-4
item.dc:creator: Associated Press
item.description: MILWAUKEE (AP) — Jacob Misiorowski allowed two hits in 5 1/3 shutout innings to cap his brilliant season as the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the St. Louis Cardinals 6-4 on Sunday. The Brewers improved to 103-59 and closed the regular season with five straight victories, matching their longest streak of the season. item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Jacob Misiorowski allowed two hits in 5 1/3 shutout innings to cap his brilliant season as the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the St. Louis Cardinals 6-4 on Sunday.
The Brewers improved to 103-59 and closed the regular season with five straight victories, matching their longest streak of the season. The Brewers’ 103 wins broke the franchise record they had set a year earlier when they went 97-65.
Milwaukee has home-field advantage throughout the postseason as it gears up for its eighth playoff appearance in nine years.
St. Louis closed a fourth straight non-playoff season with a 77-85 record, one game worse than the Cardinals’ finish last year.
Misiorowski (16-5) struck out five and walked two while improving his ERA to 1.80, the best in the majors. Misiorowski also has an MLB-leading 252 strikeouts.
Milwaukee gave Misiorowski an early 3-0 lead when Cardinals starter Andre Pallante allowed singles to six of the first seven batters he faced. Jackson Chourio, Brice Turang and Christian Yelich each hit an RBI single.
Turang’s infield hit brought home Jake Bauers for his 100th RBI of the season. Six of them came during this weekend sweep.
Turang became the eighth player in Brewers history to have at least 100 runs and 100 RBIs in a season. Ryan Braun accomplished the feat four times. Robin Yount, Cecil Cooper and Prince Fielder did it twice each. The others are Jeromy Burnitz and John Jaha.
Gary Sánchez hit a two-run homer in the third and Chourio added a two-out RBI single in the fourth to extend the lead to 6-0. Chourio went 3 for 4.
St. Louis scored all four of its runs in the eighth inning off Chad Patrick. Leo Bernal highlighted that outburst with a three-run homer.
Shane Drohan retired the side in order in the ninth to earn his second save.
Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs and 10 hits in five innings.
Up next
The NL Central champion Brewers will host either the Chicago Cubs or San Diego Padres in the opening game of an NL Division Series on Saturday.

item.title: [New York Post] Dodgers get A grade in final Post MLB Power Rankings. But who gets an F?
item.dc:creator: Jack Harris

item.content:encoded:
Throughout the season, the California Post power-ranked MLB’s 30 teams and checked in on intriguing awards races. Records as of Saturday morning:
1) Brewers (101-59): A+
It was another perfect regular season for the Brewers, who won 100 games for the first time in franchise history to clinch the best record in the majors. Of course, their repeated failures in recent postseasons mean the real test is still to come in October. They have one superstar in Jacob Misiorowski but will need others to emerge in this year’s playoffs.
2) Dodgers (98-62): A
It was a familiar story for the Dodgers this year. A hot start. A second-half slump. Plenty of injuries along the way. Yet, another division crown that sets them up for another deep October run. That formula has worked the past two years for the two-time defending champions. Their real grade this season will depend on whether they can complete a World Series three-peat.
3) Rays (97-63): A+
After two years of missing the playoffs, the Rays had a very Rays-esque season. Uncovered gems on the mound. A relentlessly consistent lineup at the plate. And, as a result, the AL’s best record — and their best chance to get back to the World Series since 2020.
4) Braves (93-67): A
The Braves are back in the playoffs and back atop the NL East, rebounding as hoped from a disappointing 86-loss campaign last season that snapped a six-year postseason streak.
5) Yankees (93-68): B+
This grade might’ve been higher, if not for the uncertainty shrouding the Bronx Bombers as they enter the postseason. They managed to survive one extended Aaron Judge absence this regular season. Trying to do so again in October would be a tall task.
6) Padres (89-71): A-
In the weeks leading up to the trade deadline, the Padres seemed bound to be sellers. But then their offense — especially Fernando Tatis Jr. — came back to life. They bolstered their rotation by being buyers at the trade deadline instead. And now they are back in the playoffs as a potential dark horse, thanks to their 16-5 record in September.
7) Cubs (88-73): B+
The Cubs are back in the playoffs for a second straight year. They have the presumptive National League MVP in Pete Crow-Armstrong. And they managed to overcome a wave of pitching injuries. Now, they will try to mount a deeper October run after being knocked out in Game 5 of the NLDS last year.
8) Red Sox (87-74): B+
A strange regular season in Boston has reached a satisfactory ending, with the Red Sox — led by interim-now-turned-permanent manager Chad Tracy — getting a shot to avenge last year’s postseason elimination to the Yankees in next week’s wild-card series.
9) Phillies (87-73): Incomplete
Check back with us on Sunday night for this final grade. Because after seemingly salvaging their nightmarish start to the season under interim manager Don Mattingly, the Phillies are flirting with what would be a monumental September collapse, having yet to secure their place in the playoffs amid a 2-5 slump this week.
10) Diamondbacks (86-74): B-
We are only tentatively grading the Dbacks for now, thanks to their slim (but very much possible) chances of sneaking into the playoffs. If they don’t, it will be another conflicting season for the Dbacks, who have won 80-plus games in four straight seasons but still have just their surprise 2023 World Series run to show for it.
11) Guardians (84-76): A
The Guardians did what they do this season. Prevent runs. Score just enough. Fly under the radar for most of the year. Then round into form late to (most likely) win another AL Central title.
12) White Sox (83-77): A
This could still become an A+ if the White Sox wind up winning the AL Central. But even if not, the South Siders have been the most pleasant surprise in the majors this season, going from three straight 100-loss seasons to an upstart playoff berth with their young and promising roster.
13/14) Astros/Rangers (79-81): Incomplete
To be clear, neither of these teams has had a good 2026. And yet, they both enter the final days of the season with a chance to win the AL West — even though they can finish no better than .500. It will be the first time in MLB history a team will make the playoffs without a winning record. What a year in the AL West.
15) Pirates (81-79): C+
Good news: The Pirates avoided a losing record for the first time since 2018. Bad news: It wasn’t enough to keep them in playoff contention despite a surprisingly productive year from their offense.
16) Marlins (79-81): C+
The Marlins flirted with playoff contention for a while before ultimately fading down the stretch. They could be poised to take another step next year. Then again, they’ve looked that way before (remember that surprise playoff appearance in 2023?) and been unable to keep progressing.
17) Orioles (79-82): D
The Orioles’ signing of Pete Alonso worked out. But little else did in Baltimore this year. The once-budding contender has now missed the playoffs in two straight years after being swept in back-to-back postseasons the two years before that.
18) Blue Jays (78-82): D
As if the Blue Jays’ post-pennant campaign wasn’t bad enough, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. provided one more low point with his comments about his $500 million contract this week. There is hope for next season. But this year stung.
19) Cardinals (77-83): B
Given nonexistent preseason expectations, the rebuilding Cardinals mostly accomplished what they wanted to this year. They have young talent in Jordan Walker and JJ Wetherholt. They have rebuilt what is now a highly ranked farm system. And they look like a team capable of making a jump in 2027 and beyond.
20) Nationals (76-84): C
The Nats were never serious playoff contenders (their MLB-record 42 blown saves made sure of that). But they have identified a core of young talent to build around. Whether they will spend to add the necessary pieces around them, however, remains to be seen.
21) Mets (73-87): D-
The Mets can only hope this train wreck of a year serves as some sort of cleanse as they look to retool their roster this winter. The only thing that saved this from being an F was their second-half performance under another interim-now-turned-permanent manager in Andy Green.
22) Twins (76-84): C
For some reason, the Twins were intent on being playoff contenders this year. For a while, they hung around in a bad AL wild-card race. But in the end, they’ve wound up back where they started: With an OK, but not-at-all contending, roster that leaves them stuck in MLB’s no-man’s land.
23) Tigers (75-85): D
How much will the Tigers rue their decision to not maximize Tarik Skubal’s trade value by dealing him last winter? It could depend, first and foremost, on River Ryan’s development in their rotation. At the least, he offered signs of promise with a scoreless three-inning debut with the team this week.
24) Reds (74-86): D
Whatever momentum the Reds thought they were building after last year’s postseason berth vanished this summer, despite Elly De La Cruz cementing himself as one of the best players in baseball. The next time their owner asks why they aren’t the Brewers, someone should hold up a mirror.
25) Mariners (74-86): F
At the beginning of the year, only the Dodgers had a higher probability of making the playoffs (according to FanGraphs’ computer models) than the Mariners’ 80.9% mark. Instead, they suffered what might be the most disappointing season in their long-tortured history. They could be good again next year. But this season was a reminder that’s anything but a guarantee.
26) Royals (68-92): D
Another disastrous Royals season leaves them facing an existential crisis, trying to figure out how to return to competitiveness before they waste the prime of Bobby Witt Jr.’s career.
27) Giants (65-95): F
The Giants thought they could be contenders this year. Instead, they now find themselves at a crossroads. They have little choice but to run it back with their thus-far disappointing core of Willy Adames, Matt Chapman and Rafael Devers (plus Logan Webb). But this year, they looked a long way off from even being competitive.
28) Athletics (64-96): D-
There was some thought before the year that the Athletics’ young roster could be feisty. Now, the only question is how much longer they have to waste away in their minor-league ballpark purgatory.
29) Angels (62-98): C
This grade has little to do with the Angels’ on-field product, as they flirt with what would be the first 100-loss season in franchise history, and everything to do with the changes they’ve made behind the scenes. New owner. New front office. And for the first time in a while, new reason for long-term hope.
30) Rockies (57-103): D
The best thing we can say about the Rockies: They proved slightly tougher to beat during this 100-loss season, as opposed to each of the three previous ones they have suffered the last three years. Progress!
Awards Predictions
NL MVP: Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs
AL MVP: Yordan Alvarez, Astros
NL Cy Young: Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers
AL Cy Young: Cam Schlittler, Yankees
NL Rookie of the Year: Sal Stewart, Reds
AL Rookie of the Year: Kevin McGonigle, Tigers
NL Reliever of the Year: Mason Miller, Padres
AL Reliever of the Year: Louis Varland, Blue Jays

item.title: [Reviewing the Brew] Brewers’ Jacob Misiorowski chasing rare franchise history in addition to Cy Young pursuit
item.dc:creator: Evan Frederiksen
item.description: Just one regular-season series against their division rivals, the St. Louis Cardinals, remains in what has been the most successful regular season in Milwaukee Brewers history. A team that many experts picked to finish with 80-85 wins has already reached the 100-win mark with three games left to play in the regular season. With a first-round bye, the top seed in the National League, and home-field advantage throughout the postseason, the Brewers have set themselves up for success for in the play
item.content:encoded:
Just one regular-season series against their division rivals, the St. Louis Cardinals, remains in what has been the most successful regular season in Milwaukee Brewers history. A team that many experts picked to finish with 80-85 wins has already reached the 100-win mark with three games left to play in the regular season. With a first-round bye, the top seed in the National League, and home-field advantage throughout the postseason, the Brewers have set themselves up for success for in the playoffs just as they did a season ago.
However, while the 2025 and 2026 Brewers both achieved the best regular season record in MLB, there's a key difference between the two teams that should have fans feeling more confident in this year's club: The 2026 squad will be led by the best pitcher in baseball, Jacob Misiorowski. Yes, the 2025 team had an ace in Freddy Peralta, who put together the best season of his career last year, but there's no denying that Misiorowski is in a different tier.
Thanks to a sophomore season breakout, the 24-year-old flame-throwing Misiorowski is the clear front-runner for the 2026 NL Cy Young Award. Just one year ago, when the Brewers were deciding whether or not to include Misiorowski on their postseason roster due to his late-season command issues and concerning inconsistency, the thought of Miz running away with the Cy Young in 2026 seemed far-fetched. The dominant right-hander, however, has reached his ceiling far quicker than anyone expected him to, and, as a result, is just weeks away from adding a Cy Young Award to a resume that already includes two All-Star Game appearances.
In pursuit of the National League's top pitcher honor, Misiorowski is unsurprisingly on the verge of etching his name in the franchise record books as well. One impressive franchise record looks all but certain after Miz's memorable 2026 campaign.
Jacob Misiorowski on the verge of setting a new single-season franchise record for the lowest ERA by a starting pitcher
Misiorowski is scheduled to make one more start before the end of the season in Sunday afternoon's season finale against the St. Louis Cardinals. While Miz's most recent start, which came against the Baltimore Orioles, lasted just three innings by design, it's possible the Brewers let their ace go a little deeper on Sunday, as he prepares for his expected start in Game 1 of the NLDS on the following Saturday.
His preparation for the postseason is undoubtedly the most important aspect for Miz in his final start of the regular season, but as the flame-thrower's attention remains locked in on the playoffs, Brewers fans may witness some incredible franchise history. Misiorowski currently sports an otherworldly 1.86 ERA, which is best in baseball this year -- New York Yankee's right-hander Cam Schlittler is in second with a 1.96. However, it's not just the best ERA in baseball that Miz is vying for, which would make him the second Brewer to win an ERA title (Corbin Burnes, 2021); Misiorowski also has a good chance to post the lowest season-long ERA by a qualified starter in franchise history.
The current leader for the lowest single-season ERA in franchise history is Mike Caldwell, whose 2.36 ERA during his incredible 1978 season barely tops the 2.43 mark Burnes posted in 2021. Assuming Miz covers five innings on Sunday, the Brewers' ace would have to allow 11 earned runs to fall behind Caldwell's franchise record.
To make matters even more impressive, given the command troubles that plagued Misiorowski a season ago, the flame-thrower has a chance to set a new franchise record for the lowest WHIP (walks + hits per inning pitched) in a single season. Miz's 2026 WHIP with one start to go is 0.803, and the lowest to this point in franchise history is the 0.940 WHIP Burnes posted in 2021. Pair that with the fact that Misiorowski looks all but certain to set a new franchise mark for strikeouts per nine innings pitched, and it becomes even clearer just how dominant Miz's 2026 campaign truly has been.
For Misiorowski, the 2026 season has been the result of his growth as a pitcher. His one-of-a-kind velocity is certainly the driving factor that catches everyone's attention, but his improved secondary offerings and far better command are why hitters just haven’t been able to come up with any answers. With a chance to make rare baseball and Brewers history, Misiorowski will have one final opportunity to put the cherry on top of what has been a remarkable season for both himself and the Brewers.

item.title: [sportingnews.com] Diamondbacks' Ketel Marte gets dubious 'LVP' label from MLB analyst | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Matt Sullivan
item.description: The Arizona Diamondbacks are fighting for a postseason spot, with only the Philadelphia Phillies within reach heading into the final few days of the regular season. There are a lot of players who've helped the Diamondbacks get to this point, but they have also dealt with others who've held the team back, whether it's due to an injury or poor play. Or, in the case of Jayson Stark of The Athletic's "LVP" in the NL for the 2026 season, Ketel Marte, it's off-field drama and underwhelming at-best pro
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Diamondbacks are fighting for a postseason spot, with only the Philadelphia Phillies within reach heading into the final few days of the regular season.
There are a lot of players who've helped the Diamondbacks get to this point, but they have also dealt with others who've held the team back, whether it's due to an injury or poor play.
Or, in the case of Jayson Stark of The Athletic's "LVP" in the NL for the 2026 season, Ketel Marte, it's off-field drama and underwhelming at-best production. Marte was named by Stark as the "Least Valuable Player" in the NL for the 2026 season.
Ketel Marte called NL's 'LVP' for 2026 season
Marte earned Stark's LVP nomination for the National League thanks to a few different problems he's been a part of this season.
One of the biggest, most glaring issues for Marte was his unexpected absence from the team during their series against the Boston Red Sox.
He left the team on his own, was placed on the restricted list, and was seen in the casino late at night, not far from where his Diamondbacks' teammates were playing that same night.
Unfortunately, it's not just that whole debacle that explains why Marte is the Least Valuable Player in the NL this season, according to Stark.
"... Marte's on-base percentage is down more than 60 points from last year ... and his slugging percentage has dropped by over 80 points -- and his wRC+ (102) tells us he is basically just a league-average player, after two straight years in which he was about 50 percent better than league average. Not good," Stark writes.
Marte has posted 2.3 bWAR this season in 138 games played, hitting .250 with a .316 on-base percentage and a .435 slugging percentage.
His .893 OPS from the 2025 season has dropped considerably to a .752 OPS this season. That's a 141-point drop over one year.
Marte went from being a superstar who could carry the Diamondbacks if needed to just being a slightly above-average player.
While Marte hasn't been terrible, his off-field drama combined with a major offensive regression has made it clear that Marte has been a major disappointment this season.
Stark named him the NL's "Least Valuable Player" for the 2026 season. It's an unfortunate label, one that he's earned after quite the tumultuous 2026 season.
More MLB news:

- Kyle Schwarber and Colson Montgomery are in a race for MLB history no one wants to make
- White Sox reportedly have 'no urgency' to sign Munetaka Murakami to an extension
